evidence: Cic. Sen. 46: quī paucī admodum restant
terms.comment: What is left is the subject, and the person it is left to goes in the dative: nihil mihi restat. “It remains to …” is restat ut with the subjunctive (Traupman 370; Cic. N. D. 2.44, Lewis & Short).

evidence: Phaedr. 3 epil. 1: supersunt mihi quae scrībam
terms.comment: Quod superest, as for the rest (Cic. Att. 9.19.3, Lewis & Short).

evidence: Cic. Fam. 9.18.4: mūlō istō, quem tibi reliquum dīcis esse
terms.comment: Reliquum est ut, it remains that; reliquī, the rest, the others.

phrases.latin: roget quid operis siet factum, quid restet
phrases.english: let him ask what work has been done and what is left

phrases.latin: potes mūlō istō, quem tibi reliquum dīcis esse, quoniam canthērium comēdistī, Rōmam pervehī
phrases.english: you can ride to Rome on that mule you say you have left, since you have eaten your horse

phrases.latin: supersunt mihi quae scrībam, sed parcō sciēns
phrases.english: I have more left to write, but I stop on purpose

resto.html: A compound of stō and the prefix re- (de Vaan 516, s.v. re-, red-). Lewis & Short writes rē- before sc, sp and st, and only there. Its article on the prefix gives rĕ, with a by-form rĕd-, and puts the poets’ rēdūcō, rēlātum down to “the suppression of the d”; the long mark before s and a consonant seems to rest on the same idea, as its dī-scindō from dis- does. Bennett (The Latin Language §48) rejects that lengthening for ascendō, distinguō, suspiciō as “an untenable theory of compensatory lengthening”, and Lewis’s own Elementary Latin Dictionary (1890) prints re-spondeō.
